title: Polymyalgia Rheumatica
summary: Manage suspected polymyalgia rheumatica by excluding concurrent giant cell arteritis and mimics before committing to prolonged glucocorticoids, then use individualized prednisone tapering with serial assessment of disease activity, inflammatory markers, and treatment toxicity.
seoDescription: Physician guide to diagnosing and treating polymyalgia rheumatica, recognizing giant cell arteritis, excluding mimics, and tapering prednisone.
clinicalQuestion: How should clinicians confirm, treat, taper, and monitor polymyalgia rheumatica while avoiding missed giant cell arteritis and diagnostic mimics?
keyTakeaways: Before treating presumed PMR, actively screen for giant cell arteritis; headache, visual symptoms, scalp tenderness, temporal artery abnormalities, or ischemic symptoms shift management toward urgent GCA evaluation rather than routine PMR treatment. [1][20]

PMR remains a clinical diagnosis supported by inflammatory markers and longitudinal response; use the 2012 EULAR/ACR criteria as classification support, not as a substitute for exclusion of mimics. [7][12][23]

Oral glucocorticoids are standard initial therapy; a commonly described standardized starting regimen is prednisone 15 mg/day, with diagnosis reassessed when the expected clinical course is not achieved. [7]

Individualize glucocorticoid tapering and monitor disease activity, laboratory markers, and adverse events regularly; taper to prednisone 10 mg/day within 4-8 weeks, then by 1 mg every 4 weeks if remission persists. [3]
At relapse, return prednisone to the pre-relapse dose, then reduce gradually over 4-8 weeks to the dose at which relapse occurred. [3]
Monitor actively for glucocorticoid complications, including hypertension, osteoporosis, weight gain, cataracts, insomnia, bruising, and skin thinning. [20]

sections.heading: Separate isolated PMR from giant cell arteritis before routine treatment
sections.intro: The first decision is whether the presentation may represent GCA with an ischemic complication.
paragraphs: At every initial PMR assessment, ask specifically about new localized headache, scalp tenderness, temporal artery tenderness or reduced pulse, visual change or visual loss, and other ischemia-related symptoms. These are cranial GCA features used in FDA-reviewed GCA trial eligibility criteria and should trigger urgent GCA-directed assessment rather than an assumption of uncomplicated PMR. [1]

Check for a PMR-GCA overlap even when the presenting complaint is proximal stiffness: PMR features are present in 40%-60% of patients with GCA at diagnosis, and approximately 22% of patients with PMR have concurrent GCA reported in referral literature. [4][11] A patient with visual symptoms, new headache, scalp tenderness, or fever should not be managed solely with a low-dose PMR glucocorticoid regimen. [1][20]

Age helps frame the differential but does not establish the diagnosis. PMR is a disorder of older adults; age younger than 50 years is an atypical feature that should intensify evaluation for an alternative explanation of polymyalgic symptoms. [7][9]
bullets: Document GCA screen at baseline: new localized headache, scalp tenderness, temporal artery tenderness or diminished pulse, visual symptoms or vision loss, and fever. [1][20]

If cranial or ischemic GCA features are present, expedite specialist-directed GCA evaluation; do not use a clinical response to moderate-dose prednisone as reassurance that GCA has been excluded. [1][11]
If no GCA features are present, proceed with a structured PMR workup and reassess the diagnosis during follow-up. [7][12]

sections.heading: Confirm a polymyalgic syndrome, then test the competing diagnoses
sections.intro: Use criteria and treatment response to support—not replace—clinical exclusion of mimics.
paragraphs: Use the 2012 EULAR/ACR provisional classification criteria as a structured aid in patients with suspected PMR; the ACR lists these criteria as PMR classification criteria. [23] They are not a definitive diagnostic test: retrospective validation work found that a modified version can identify valid PMR diagnoses in surveys, while the broader diagnostic literature emphasizes a polymyalgic syndrome that may arise from PMR or another disease. [7][12]

Obtain ESR and CRP at baseline and interpret them as part of a syndrome-level assessment, not as standalone proof. In a pivotal GCA program, historical ESR at least 50 mm/hour or CRP at least 2.45 mg/dL was used as an inflammatory entry criterion for GCA, underscoring why elevated acute-phase reactants in a patient with polymyalgic symptoms should also prompt an explicit GCA screen. [1] ESR below 40 mm/hour or above 100 mm/hour is an atypical PMR pattern that warrants renewed attention to alternatives. [9]

The principal diagnostic safeguard is deliberate consideration of inflammatory rheumatic disease, systemic infection, and malignancy. Rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory articular diseases can present with a polymyalgic syndrome, while systemic infections and malignancy can mimic PMR. [7][9] Limited or asymmetric involvement of the usual sites, age under 50 years, and discordant ESR values are practical flags to pause before initiating a prolonged PMR treatment course. [9]

Musculoskeletal ultrasound can increase the specificity of the 2012 EULAR/ACR criteria when distinguishing PMR from rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory articular diseases. [9] Reserve PET/CT for selected unresolved cases or when another process remains plausible; it can assist in differentiating PMR/GCA from mimics but entails substantial cost, with an average Medicare reimbursement cited at approximately $1,377. [2]
bullets: Record baseline ESR and CRP before treatment when this does not delay care for suspected GCA. [1][3]
Use targeted examination and history to identify peripheral inflammatory arthritis or other findings that favor rheumatoid arthritis or another inflammatory arthropathy. [7][9]
Broaden the evaluation for infection or malignancy when the pattern is atypical or the subsequent clinical course is inconsistent with PMR. [7][9]
Use musculoskeletal ultrasound when discrimination from rheumatoid arthritis or another inflammatory articular disease is a key unresolved question. [9]

subsections.heading: Use treatment response as longitudinal diagnostic evidence
paragraphs: A standardized approach described in diagnostic literature uses prednisone 15 mg/day, but durable diagnostic confidence develops through follow-up rather than through a single steroid-response test. One review describes confirmation only after 12-18 months of treatment, full recovery, and discontinuation of glucocorticoids. [7] Failure to achieve or maintain the anticipated course should reopen the differential rather than automatically prompt escalating glucocorticoid exposure. [7][9]

sections.heading: Start oral glucocorticoids and prescribe the taper at the same visit
sections.intro: The therapeutic objective is disease control with the lowest sustainable glucocorticoid exposure.
paragraphs: Oral glucocorticoid therapy is the standard treatment for established PMR. [7][8][24] A diagnostic-treatment approach describes prednisone 15 mg/day as the standardized initial regimen; this dose applies to suspected isolated PMR, not to patients in whom GCA remains a concern. [7]

Individualize the starting plan and subsequent taper according to disease activity, laboratory markers, comorbidities, and treatment adverse events. The EULAR/ACR management recommendation strongly endorses individualized tapering with regular monitoring of all three domains. [3] This is particularly important in older adults, in whom even low-dose corticosteroids can cause clinically meaningful toxicity. [20]

For initial tapering, reduce to prednisone-equivalent 10 mg/day within 4-8 weeks. [3] Once remission is achieved, reduce by 1 mg/day every 4 weeks until discontinuation if remission is maintained; an alternative cited approach uses 1.25-mg decrements through alternating daily schedules such as 10 mg and 7.5 mg on alternate days. [3]

Treat clinical relapse by increasing prednisone to the pre-relapse dose, then gradually reducing over 4-8 weeks to the dose at which relapse occurred. [3] Do not use a rigid taper when symptoms, inflammatory markers, or adverse events argue for a different pace; the recommendation specifically prioritizes regular reassessment over a fixed schedule. [3]
bullets: Initial regimen described for PMR: prednisone 15 mg/day. [7]
Initial taper target: prednisone-equivalent 10 mg/day by 4-8 weeks. [3]
Maintenance taper in sustained remission: decrease by 1 mg/day every 4 weeks. [3]
Relapse: return to the pre-relapse dose, then reduce over 4-8 weeks to the relapse dose. [3]
Do not extrapolate an isolated-PMR dose strategy to a patient with possible GCA. [1][20]

sections.heading: Monitor relapse, reconsider the diagnosis, and prevent treatment harm
sections.intro: Each follow-up visit should assess active disease, emergent GCA, and cumulative steroid toxicity.
paragraphs: At follow-up, assess clinical disease activity, repeat the laboratory markers used at baseline, and review adverse events at intervals matched to the taper. [3] A rising inflammatory marker without concordant symptoms should not by itself define relapse, but discordance between symptoms, markers, and the expected taper trajectory should trigger reassessment for an alternative diagnosis or concurrent GCA. [3][7][9]

Repeat the GCA symptom screen throughout treatment: headache, visual changes, scalp tenderness, temporal artery findings, and fever remain management-changing symptoms because PMR may coexist with GCA. [1][4][20] New visual symptoms or ischemic features require urgent escalation rather than adjustment of a routine PMR taper. [1]

Build glucocorticoid toxicity surveillance into every visit. The ACR patient guidance identifies hypertension, osteoporosis, weight gain, cataracts, insomnia, bruising, and skin thinning as adverse effects requiring regular check-ups, and notes that older patients may require osteoporosis medications to prevent fractures. [20] A taper that controls symptoms but produces unacceptable toxicity should be revisited using the guideline principle of individualized dosing and adverse-event monitoring. [3][20]

Reopen the diagnostic process when response is incomplete, relapse occurs repeatedly, inflammatory markers are atypical, or the symptom distribution becomes asymmetric or limited. PMR is not confirmed simply because symptoms transiently improve on prednisone; rheumatic disorders, infection, and malignancy can present as a polymyalgic syndrome and may declare themselves during follow-up. [7][9]
bullets: At each visit: document stiffness and functional trajectory, assess GCA symptoms, review ESR/CRP in clinical context, and screen for glucocorticoid adverse effects. [3][20]
Escalate promptly for new headache, visual symptoms, scalp tenderness, temporal artery abnormalities, or fever. [1][20]
Consider osteoporosis-prevention treatment in older adults receiving corticosteroids, particularly when fracture risk warrants it. [20]
Reassess for rheumatoid arthritis or other inflammatory arthropathy, infection, or malignancy when the clinical course is not convincingly PMR. [7][9]
